analysis.one_liner: Strips states of the power to set animal-welfare and production standards for food sold across state lines.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred states from imposing their own standards on out-of-state food production, never received a committee vote and died when Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would prohibit states and local governments from imposing any standard on how agricultural products are raised or produced in other states if that standard goes beyond federal law and the law of the state where production happens. It would also let anyone affected — including producers, trade associations, and governments — sue in federal court to invalidate such state rules and recover damages, and courts would generally have to freeze enforcement of the state rule while the case is pending. The practical target was state standards like California's measure requiring more space for pigs and egg-laying hens.
analysis.who_benefits: Large livestock, pork, and egg producers who confine animals would gain, because they could sell into any state without meeting that state's stricter animal-welfare or production rules. National food retailers and processors would also gain by not having to track different standards for different states, and trade associations would gain a new federal lawsuit tool against state regulations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large confinement livestock and egg producers

how_it_helps.text: Producers in states with few restrictions could sell into strict states like California without changing how they raise animals, since no state could impose standards on production occurring elsewhere beyond federal law [S2][S3].

The bill creates a private right of action allowing producers, transporters, trade associations, and even governments to sue to invalidate state agricultural regulations and collect damages for economic loss, with a mandatory preliminary injunction freezing enforcement unless the state proves its case by clear and convincing evidence [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State voters and consumers would bear the cost: rules they adopted — often by ballot initiative — to require more humane treatment of farm animals or stricter production conditions could be invalidated, and states would face waves of litigation and automatic injunctions. Small producers who already invested in meeting higher-welfare standards could be undercut by cheaper confinement-raised products.

drawbacks.text: The bill would override standards that state voters and legislatures adopted through their own democratic processes, including voter-approved measures, because it bars any state from setting conditions on out-of-state production beyond federal law [S2][S3].

The private right of action runs for ten years and entitles challengers to a preliminary injunction unless the state proves it will likely prevail by clear and convincing evidence, an unusually demanding standard that would effectively suspend state rules during litigation [S3].

A good-faith objection from the bill's supporters' side is that a patchwork of differing state production standards raises costs for farmers and could raise food prices; opponents reply that states have long regulated goods sold in interstate commerce and that federal law remains the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's gains flow mainly to large producers who want to avoid meeting stricter state rules, while the costs fall on states' ability to set their own food-production standards, on consumers who chose those rules, and on farmers who already complied. The bill offers nothing directly to ordinary people; its public-facing argument is lower prices from uniform standards, which the record does not quantify.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture and Judiciary committees in June 2023, no committee ever acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ashley Hinson introduced the bill on June 30, 2023, with 37 Republican cosponsors [S1][S4].
The bill was sent to both the Agriculture Committee and the Judiciary Committee, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
It never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either chamber, and expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, states and their voters keep the power to set food-production standards, and the large producers the bill would have freed from those rules gained nothing. Nothing changed for anyone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: States, their voters, and higher-welfare farmers

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-controlled committees [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large pork, egg, and poultry producers using confinement systems
industries.note: The bill would have let them sell confinement-raised products into states that require more humane conditions, avoiding the cost of complying with rules like California's Proposition 12. Consumers in those states would lose the standards they voted for.

A single federal floor instead of differing state rules simplifies sourcing and cuts compliance costs for national supply chains. The trade-off is that shopper-chosen standards no longer shape what is sold.

industries.industry: Farmers who already meet higher-welfare state standards
industries.note: Producers who invested in cage-free or crate-free systems could be undercut by cheaper out-of-state products raised under weaker rules.
States would lose regulatory authority over out-of-state agricultural production and face a ten-year private right of action with automatic injunctions against their rules.
